analysis.one_liner: Raises the excise tax on corporate stock buybacks from 1% to 4% and closes an executive-stock loophole.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in June 2026 and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where no hearing, markup, or vote has been scheduled; no Republicans have signed on.
analysis.plain_summary: Corporations already pay a 1% federal tax when they repurchase their own stock — buybacks, which return cash to shareholders instead of investing or raising pay. This bill would quadruple that tax to 4%. It would also stop companies from lowering the tax by counting stock they issue to executives and other employees earning over $1 million a year. The bill has gone no further than committee referral.
analysis.who_benefits: If passed, the federal treasury gains revenue from the higher tax, and the tax pressure tilts slightly against companies returning all spare cash to shareholders through buybacks rather than investment or wages. Workers and retirement savers benefit only indirectly, through a modest shift in corporate behavior and added revenue.

how_it_helps.text: Quadruples the excise tax on corporate stock repurchases from 1% to 4%, effective for repurchases after enactment [S2].

Removes an offset that currently lets companies reduce the buyback tax by the value of stock they issue during the year, when that stock goes to covered executives or to anyone earning over $1 million in compensation from the company [S2].
Includes special transition rules for the tax year containing enactment so companies cannot pre-load repurchases or stock issuance to dodge the new rate [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Large public corporations that buy back their own stock pay the 4% excise, and their shareholders — including mutual funds and pension funds holding the stock — ultimately bear the cost. Companies that rely on stock-based pay for high earners also lose the offset.

drawbacks.text: A buyback tax can be sidestepped: companies can return cash through dividends instead of repurchases, or time transactions around the rules, so the revenue raised may be smaller than the headline rate suggests (general knowledge about how buyback taxes work).

The tax falls on the stock itself, so costs spread across all shareholders — including pension funds and 401(k) investors holding broad index funds — not only on the executives and large holders the bill's design targets.
The bill raises a tax rate but leaves buybacks fully legal and the underlying tax in place, so its effect on corporate behavior would likely be modest relative to total buyback volume.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow tool: a higher excise tax plus a fix aimed at executive stock offsets. The revenue and behavioral effect would be real but modest, and the cost lands broadly on shareholders, including ordinary retirement savers. It is not a sweeping change to how corporations operate, and supporters should be honest that avoidance channels remain open.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Finance Committee on the day it was introduced, and no hearing, markup, or vote has happened since.

narrative.text: Introduced June 16, 2026 by Senator Schumer with six additional Democratic cosponsors listed on the bill [S1].
Read twice in the Senate and referred to the Committee on Finance the same day; that referral is the only recorded action since [S4].
As of the record, no committee action, floor vote, or House counterpart action has been scheduled [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, large corporations and their shareholders are better off: the buyback excise remains at 1% and the executive-stock offset remains intact, because the bill has not advanced.

for.name: Sen. Charles Schumer
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and put his name on the fourfold buyback tax increase [S1].

for.name: Sen. Ron Wyden
for.role: Senator and Finance Committee member; cosponsor
for.what_they_did: Signed on as a cosponsor; he is widely reported as the architect of the original 1% buyback excise tax enacted in 2022.

for.name: Six additional Democratic senators
for.role: Cosponsors (Warren, Reed, Van Hollen, Markey, Whitehouse, and one more)
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, giving it 8 Democratic sponsors and no others [S3].

sides.party_line_note: The sponsor and all seven cosponsors are Democrats, with no Republican support on record, and the bill sits in the Senate Finance Committee, which Republicans chair.

industries.industry: Large public corporations and their shareholders
industries.note: The bill quadruples their buyback excise tax and removes the offset for executive stock issuance. The cost lands on corporate cash reserves and shareholder returns, including retirement funds that hold the stock.

industries.industry: Highly compensated executives and covered employees
industries.note: Stock the company issues to executives and $1-million-plus earners can no longer reduce the company's buyback tax, making executive equity pay slightly more costly to the firm.

industries.industry: Corporate law and tax advisory firms
industries.note: New effective-date rules, proration formulas, and a new exception create planning work for companies seeking to manage the tax.

analysis.trajectory: Most tax bills referred to the Senate Finance Committee without bipartisan cosponsorship never get a hearing or markup, especially in a committee led by the other party. Unless Democrats attach it to a larger tax package or gain Republican support, this bill is likely to sit without action for the rest of the 119th Congress.
